common_name: Nana Rosea Lavender (Dwarf Pink English Lavender)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in full sun with sharp drainage; this is a true dwarf selection, so keep it to the front of the border or in pots where its small scale won't be lost among larger perennials.

directions: Nana Rosea forms a tight, rounded mound of narrow silver-gray foliage noticeably smaller than standard English lavenders, topped in summer with short spikes of soft pale pink flowers rather than the usual blue-violet. Grow it in lean, neutral-to-alkaline soil with excellent drainage, since this dwarf habit is especially prone to crown rot if water sits around the base. Its small size makes it well suited to edging paths, rock gardens, and containers where a full-sized lavandin would overwhelm the space. Trim lightly after bloom to keep the mound dense and prevent the woody base from becoming sparse and leggy over time.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring, spacing generously in rows if grown for cut flowers or distillation; like other lavandin clones it needs a full growing season to establish before its first substantial harvest.

directions: Super is one of the classic French lavandin clones selected for essential oil production alongside 'Grosso' and 'Abrialii', valued for its abundant, long-stemmed violet-blue flower spikes and a fragrance considered finer and less camphorous than other lavandin clones. Grow in full sun on lean, fast-draining, slightly alkaline soil, since this large hybrid lavender resents heavy or wet ground far more than true English lavender. The vigorous, rounded clumps produce heavy flower yields useful for cutting, drying, and craft or sachet work even outside commercial oil production. Shear the whole plant back by about a third right after flowering to maintain a dense form and prevent the woody base from splitting open in later years.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in full sun with sharp drainage; give it the same generous spacing as other lavandin clones since mature plants form a wide, rounded clump.

directions: Seal is a long-standing lavandin clone grown for its abundant pale violet flower spikes carried well above the foliage on tall, leafless stems, and its soft, long-lasting fragrance makes it a favorite for sachets and dried lavender bags. Grow in lean, fast-draining, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, where the broad silver-gray foliage mound stays tidy and the flower stems stand upright without staking. It flowers a touch later in the season than 'Grosso' or 'Provence', extending the lavender bloom window where more than one lavandin clone is planted together. Cut the spent flower spikes back hard after bloom to keep the woody framework compact and encourage strong new growth the following year.

planting.note: Start seed indoors under light several weeks ahead of the last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed; Lavance is a seed-propagated series bred to flower uniformly in its first year, unlike most named lavenders that are vegetatively propagated.

directions: Lavance Purple is a compact, uniform English lavender bred from seed to bloom reliably in its first season, carrying deep blue-purple flower spikes on upright stalks above tidy gray-green foliage. Grow in full sun with lean, sharply drained soil, since this series is bred for garden and landscape performance but still rots quickly in heavy or waterlogged ground. Its even habit and first-year flowering make it useful for mass plantings and borders where matched-size plants are wanted without waiting years for named vegetative cultivars to fill in. Shear lightly after the first flush of bloom to encourage a tidier shape and a possible rebloom later in the season.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring after frost danger passes, in full sun with sharp drainage; Willow Vale is among the hardier Spanish lavenders but still benefits from a sheltered spot at the cold edge of its range.

directions: Willow Vale is a vigorous, free-flowering Spanish lavender bred by Walberton Nursery and recognized with the RHS Award of Garden Merit, prized for its deep blue-violet flower heads topped with a showy tuft of purple petal-like bracts that rise on long, leafless stalks well above the silver-gray foliage. It blooms earlier in the season than most lavandin types and continues intermittently into fall where summers are long. Grow in full sun on lean, fast-draining soil and avoid rich or constantly moist ground, which shortens its life considerably. This selection is noted as one of the more cold-tolerant Spanish lavenders, but a winter mulch or sheltered siting is still worthwhile at the northern edge of its hardiness range.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit records

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in full sun to light afternoon shade with sharp drainage; Avonview tolerates heat and dry spells well once rooted but is not reliably hardy in cold winters.

directions: Avonview carries vivid dark blue-violet flower heads crowned with contrasting purple-violet bracts, held on long stems above soft, bright greenish-gray foliage, and it is a hybrid drawing on the rare Lavandula viridis in its parentage. It flowers through the warm months and can bloom nearly year-round in mild, frost-free climates, making it a strong choice for hot, dry gardens where many lavenders struggle. Grow in full sun with excellent drainage, and avoid rich or constantly damp soil, which quickly shortens the plant's life. Trim back lightly after each flowering flush to keep the rounded habit tidy and to encourage continued bloom through the season.
